script.opening: (Carol leads, Harold gazing at the screen.) "Thank you for calling back so fast, doctor. The carers tested his water and it’s an infection — it’s happened before and antibiotics sorted it. Can we just get them started today? I don’t want this turning into anything."

facts.text: Harold is vaguer in the evenings, "not himself" — but rousable, knows Carol, no falls. Strong dark smelly urine; dribbling small amounts often, damp patches; no burning if Harold is asked directly ("it doesn’t hurt, it just won’t come proper").
Only if asked: bowels not opened for FIVE days — "they’ve been lazy since the new painkillers". Belly feels "full". Harold rubs his lower abdomen when it’s mentioned.

Co-codamol started 3 weeks ago by a locum for shoulder pain. Taking the full QDS dose. Pain better; bowels and waterworks worse since — Carol says in passing "he’s not been right since those new painkillers" without connecting it.
Drinks "two or three cups of tea a day". Avoiding drinking deliberately — "so I don’t leak". Skin dry, lips dry on camera.

Only if her fear is noticed: her husband Derek went into hospital "with a chest" in winter 2021 and died there ten days later — she never got to sit with him. "They don’t come out of there at his age, doctor." The antibiotics are her shield against the hospital.
Two weeks ago Harold was doing the crossword and walking to the paper shop. This is a CHANGE, not his normal.

ice.ideas: Carol: positive dipstick = infection = antibiotics, like before. Harold: "my works are just old".
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — Carol is terrified of hospital admission: Derek died in hospital without her. Any plan that smells of "sending him in" will be fought. Harold’s quiet fear: the damp patches mean "the end of managing on my own".
ice.expectations: Carol: antibiotics today, no hospital, no fuss. Harold: not to be talked over.

cues: "He’s not been right since those new painkillers" — dropped in passing; the case key, unnoticed by the speaker.
Harold rubs his lower belly and winces when bowels are mentioned — on camera, wordless.
Carol’s voice cracks on "you hear what happens to people his age in there" — Derek, unspoken.

checkpoints.text: Does not treat a dipstick: states plainly that urine dipsticks are not recommended over 65 (UKHSA) and that smelly urine alone is not an infection — up to half of older adults carry bacteria harmlessly; yet, because new incontinence and new confusion are two criteria on the UKHSA over-65 tool, sends a urine culture and keeps infection on the list while hunting other causes
Hunts the real mechanism: five days constipated on new co-codamol + deliberate fluid restriction → retention with overflow (the dribbling) and evening confusion
Acts on the drug cause: stops/steps down the co-codamol (swap to paracetamol ± topical NSAID for the shoulder), starts laxatives, sets a fluid plan that answers his leak fear
Names the video’s limits and arranges same-day in-person review: abdominal/PR examination and a bladder scan — said as completing the job, not escalating it
Talks to Harold directly, by name, not over him — and gets his version ("it won’t come proper") which unlocks the retention picture
Notices Carol’s cracked voice, asks, and lets Derek’s story be told — then SAYS the reassurance she actually needs: "everything we’re doing today is designed to treat him here at home"
Reframes antibiotics honestly: the wrong treatment isn’t a shield against hospital — it’s a delay that makes admission MORE likely
Safety-nets in plain words: cannot pass urine at all / hard swollen belly / drowsy or feverish / rigors → same-day call or 999; books tomorrow’s follow-up call himself

worked.txt: "Carol, that dipstick has done its job by getting us talking — but here’s the thing: over 65, those sticks are positive in up to half of older people with no infection at all. At Harold’s age the stick can’t tell us what’s happening. His story, an examination and a proper lab test of his urine can."
"Harold — never mind the stick. Tell me about the waterworks in your own words. Does it burn, or does it just… not come properly?"

"You said something important without noticing — he’s not been right since the new painkillers. Those tablets block the bowels; five days blocked, the bowel presses on the bladder; the bladder can’t empty; it overflows in dribbles and the backed-up system fogs his evenings. One cause, the whole picture."

"Harold, I think you’re drinking less so you leak less — and I understand it, but it’s working against you. Concentrated urine irritates the bladder and fogs the head. Let’s get the emptying fixed, and then drinking properly becomes safe again."

"Carol — when you said ‘what happens to people his age in there’, that didn’t sound like a general worry. What happened?" (Then:) "Everything we’re doing this afternoon — the examination, the bladder scan, the laxatives — is how we treat this at HOME. That’s the whole plan."

"Three things change the plan tonight, and I want you both to know them: if he can’t pass water at all, if his belly goes hard and swollen, or if he becomes drowsy, hot or shaking — ring us straight away, or 999 out of hours. Otherwise, I’m ringing you tomorrow afternoon myself."

f.learning: In the very old, "UTI" is the label that stops people thinking. UKHSA advises against dipsticks over 65 (up to half of older adults have asymptomatic bacteriuria); smelly, concentrated urine usually means dehydration, and new confusion needs a cause hunted, not a reflex antibiotic. New dribbling plus new confusion are two UKHSA over-65 criteria, so infection is not dismissed — the urine goes for culture while the other causes are examined for. Here the cause is iatrogenic: opioid-induced constipation causing retention with overflow. The hidden agenda — the daughter’s terror of hospital after her husband died there — drives the antibiotic demand, and only naming it lets the right plan land.

knowledge.guideline: UKHSA Diagnosis of urinary tract infections: quick reference tools for primary care (2025) · NICE CG103 — delirium · NICE NG109 — lower UTI prescribing · NICE NG253 — sepsis
knowledge.summary: Over 65, a positive dipstick does not diagnose infection. New evening confusion, dribbling and five days’ constipation after starting co-codamol point to opioid-induced constipation with urinary retention and overflow, and early delirium. Hunt the cause, examine the same day, and send a urine culture rather than treating a dipstick.

points.t: UKHSA: urine dipsticks are not recommended in people aged 65 and over — up to half of older adults have bacteria in the urine without infection (asymptomatic bacteriuria), which does not need antibiotics. Smelly or dark urine alone is not a UTI and often reflects dehydration.

points.h: Use symptoms and signs — and look for other causes
points.t: UKHSA over-65 tool: consider UTI with new dysuria, or two or more of new frequency or urgency, new incontinence, new or worse delirium, suprapubic pain, visible haematuria, or fever. New dribbling and new confusion overlap with retention and constipation, so exclude other causes and send a urine sample for culture before any antibiotic.

NICE CG103: identify and manage the possible causes of delirium. Here: a new opioid, five days’ constipation, likely retention, poor fluid intake — plus infection to exclude. A structured tool such as the 4AT helps document it.

Codeine commonly causes constipation (BNF) and can contribute to urinary retention; faecal loading can also impair bladder emptying. Retention with overflow presents as frequent dribbling of small volumes. Same-day in-person assessment: abdomen, PR examination and a bladder scan.

Stop or step down the co-codamol — regular paracetamol (dose per BNF) with a topical NSAID for the shoulder; start a laxative such as macrogol (dose per BNF); a fluid plan that answers his fear of leaking; catheterise if there is a significant residual volume, with urology follow-up. Antibiotics per NICE NG109 only if culture and clinical picture support infection.
Inability to pass urine, a hard distended abdomen, or drowsiness, fever or rigors: same-day assessment, with sepsis risk judged per NICE NG253 — 999 if he appears seriously unwell.

dg.d: Sought Harold’s consent and version first; acknowledged Carol’s request without acting on the dipstick.
Lives at home with carers and daily visits from Carol; previous independence; fear of losing it; Carol’s bereavement.
Same-day abdominal and PR examination, bladder scan; urine culture instead of dipstick; U&E, FBC, CRP, calcium, glucose.
Opioid-induced constipation with retention and overflow; dehydration; delirium; UTI or urosepsis; prostatic obstruction.
Asked about fever, rigors, drowsiness, falls and inability to pass urine; baseline cognition established.
Likely urinary retention with overflow due to opioid-induced constipation and poor fluid intake, with early delirium; infection not yet excluded.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: No antibiotics on a dipstick; stop co-codamol, paracetamol and topical NSAID, laxative, fluid plan; catheter if retention confirmed.
Medication review so the opioid isn’t repeated; hydration and continence; support for Carol as carer.
Same-day review; named call tomorrow; clear triggers for urgent contact or 999.

model.text: Hello, I’m Dr Morgan. Is that Carol — and Mr Finch beside you? Hello, Mr Finch. Is it alright with you if we talk about how you’ve been, with Carol here?
model.why: Greets and seeks consent from the patient himself

model.text: Harold: Harold, please. Yes, she can stay.

Carol: Thank you for calling back so fast, doctor. The carers tested his water and it’s an infection — it’s happened before and antibiotics sorted it. Can we just get them started today? I don’t want this turning into anything.
I can hear how worried you are, Carol, and I’ll make sure we have a clear plan today. I’d like to hear from Harold first, then from you, then decide together. Does that sound fair?
model.why: Agenda that includes both people and sequences them

model.text: Harold — never mind the test for a moment. Tell me about the waterworks in your own words. Does it burn, or is it something else?
model.why: Speaks to Harold directly, open question

model.text: Harold: It doesn’t hurt. It just won’t come proper. Little bits, all the time. I’ve had damp patches.
That’s really helpful, thank you. And your bowels — when did you last open them?
model.why: Targeted question that opens the constipation–retention route

model.text: Harold: (Rubs lower belly, winces.) Not for… five days? They’ve been lazy since the new painkillers. My belly feels full.
I noticed you rubbing your tummy there. Is it sore low down, just above your private parts?
model.why: Acts on the non-verbal cue — possible distended bladder

model.text: Harold: A bit. Like it wants to go and can’t.
Carol, you mentioned he’s been muddled. How is he compared with two weeks ago? Any fever, shivering, falls or drowsiness?
model.why: Establishes baseline and screens for sepsis and delirium red flags

model.text: Carol: Two weeks ago he was doing the crossword and walking to the paper shop. Now he’s vague in the evenings. No fever, no falls, and he knows me. He’s not been right since those new painkillers, really.
That’s an important point. And how much is he drinking?
model.why: Picks up the painkiller cue and checks hydration

model.text: Harold: Two or three cups of tea. I don’t drink more — so I don’t leak.
Harold, that makes sense. What worries you most about the leaking?
model.why: Explores Harold’s own concern

model.text: Harold: That it’s the end of me managing on my own.
Thank you for telling me — I think there may be a fixable reason for it, and I’ll come to that. Carol, you said you don’t want this turning into anything. What are you most worried might happen?
model.why: Acknowledges Harold, then invites Carol’s concern

model.text: Carol: (Voice cracks.) You hear what happens to people his age in there.
That sounded personal. Has something happened?
model.why: Notices the cracked voice and asks

model.text: Carol: My husband, Derek. He went in with a chest in 2021 and died ten days later. I never got to sit with him. I can’t have that happen to Dad.
I’m so sorry, Carol. That explains exactly why you want this sorted at home — and I want to be clear: everything I’m about to suggest is designed to treat Harold here, at home.
model.why: Validates the loss and gives the reassurance she needs

model.text: About the dipstick: over 65, those sticks are unreliable — up to half of older people have some bacteria in their urine without any infection. So I’d rather go on Harold’s story. And it points somewhere else. The new painkillers contain codeine, which bungs the bowels up. Five days of a full bowel can press on the bladder so it can’t empty; it overflows in little dribbles — the damp patches — and that backed-up system, plus not drinking, can fog his evenings.
model.why: Defuses the dipstick and names the likely mechanism

model.text: Carol: So it isn’t an infection?

It might not be, and antibiotics wouldn’t fix a blocked bowel or a full bladder. I can’t be sure over video, so I don’t want to guess. I’d like a doctor or nurse to see him in person this afternoon: feel his tummy, check the back passage, and scan his bladder. We’ll send a urine sample to the lab rather than rely on the stick, and do some bloods. That completes the job — it’s not sending him in.
model.why: Names video limits; same-day exam, bladder scan, culture

model.text: Carol: And if his bladder is full?

Then usually a nurse can pass a small tube to drain it, often at home or in the surgery, and the relief is quick. The wrong treatment is what would make hospital more likely — the right one keeps him here.
model.why: Reframes antibiotics honestly against her fear

model.text: Harold, the painkillers helped your shoulder but they’re causing this. I’d like to stop the co-codamol and use regular paracetamol with a rub-on anti-inflammatory gel for the shoulder instead. Would you be willing to try that?
model.why: Acts on the drug cause with Harold’s agreement

model.text: Harold: If it stops this, yes.

I’ll also start a laxative today to get the bowels moving. And the drinking — I know you’ve cut back to avoid leaking, but once the bladder can empty properly, drinking more should stop the dribbling, not cause it. Could we aim for a cup every couple of hours during the day, easing off in the evening?
model.why: Fluid plan that answers his leak fear

model.text: Harold: I can try.
Carol, could you or the carers keep a note of drinks and when his bowels open? And I’ll mark the co-codamol so it doesn’t get repeated automatically.
model.why: Shares the plan and closes the prescribing loop

model.text: Carol: Yes, I can do that.

Three things would change the plan tonight: if he can’t pass water at all, if his tummy becomes hard and swollen, or if he becomes drowsy, hot or shivery. Any of those — ring us straight away, or 111 or 999 out of hours. Otherwise I’ll ring you both tomorrow afternoon myself.
model.why: Plain-language triggers and a named follow-up

model.text: Carol: Thank you. I really thought you’d say hospital.
Harold, can you tell me in your own words what we’re going to do?
model.why: Teach-back with the patient, not just the daughter

model.text: Harold: Stop the new tablets, take the paracetamol, something for my bowels, drink more tea, and someone comes to feel my belly today.
Exactly that. Anything either of you wants to ask before we finish?
model.why: Shares the floor with both

model.text: Carol: No — thank you, doctor.

social.t: Carol, 68, visits daily and is herself grieving a husband who died in hospital; her fear shapes every request. She is entitled to a carer’s assessment (Care Act 2014).
Until two weeks ago Harold managed with carers and walked to the shop; he fears incontinence means the end of living independently. Community continence services can help once the cause is fixed.

legal.t: Mental Capacity Act 2005: assume capacity; delirium can affect it, but capacity is decision-specific and fluctuates. Involve Harold in decisions and seek his consent to discuss his care with Carol.
Once he is well, a gentle conversation about lasting power of attorney and his wishes about hospital care may help both of them.

professional.t: GMC Good practice in prescribing and managing medicines and devices (2021): review new medicines for adverse effects. Record the reaction to co-codamol and stop it being repeated automatically; feed back to the locum without blame.
New confusion cannot be safely assessed by video alone — arranging a same-day face-to-face examination is part of good clinical care, not escalation.

community.t: Care agency (fluid and bowel chart), district or practice nurse for bladder scan and catheter care, community continence service, Carers UK and Age UK for support.

redFlags: Unable to pass urine, painful distended bladder or hard swollen abdomen — urgent same-day assessment
Fever, rigors, drowsiness or rapid decline — possible sepsis, assess per NICE NG253
New confusion — cause-hunt (drugs, constipation, retention, dehydration, infection) with a structured tool such as the 4AT
psychosocial: Lives at home with carers; daughter visits daily
Harold restricts fluids to avoid leaking and fears losing independence
Carol’s husband died in hospital in 2021 — her fear of admission
ice: Ideas: Carol — “positive dipstick means infection”; Harold — “my works are just old”
Concerns: Carol — hospital, after Derek; Harold — the end of managing alone
Expectations: Carol — antibiotics today, no hospital; Harold — not to be talked over

playbook.diagnosis: Explain plainly: “The dipstick can’t tell us much at Harold’s age. His story points to the new painkillers — they’ve blocked his bowels, which can stop the bladder emptying so it dribbles, and that can make him muddled. We need to check that in person today.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Think of a blocked drain in the kitchen that makes the sink next to it back up and overflow. Unblock the drain — the bowels — and the sink — the bladder — can empty again.”

management.reflectIce: “Carol, after what happened to Derek, I understand why you want to avoid hospital. Everything we’re doing today is designed to treat your dad here, at home.”
management.psychosocial: Talk to Harold directly and answer his leak fear with a fluid plan; give Carol a practical role (fluid and bowel chart) and a named call tomorrow.
sharedPlan: Same-day in-person assessment: abdomen, PR, bladder scan; urine culture (not dipstick); U&E, FBC, CRP, calcium, glucose
Stop co-codamol; regular paracetamol and topical NSAID; laxative such as macrogol (dose per BNF); fluid plan
Catheter if significant retention, with follow-up; antibiotics per NICE NG109 only if culture and signs support infection
safetyNet: Can’t pass urine, hard swollen abdomen, drowsy, hot or shivery — ring urgently, 111 or 999 out of hours
Named GP call tomorrow afternoon; co-codamol removed from repeats

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed by the word “UTI”: it stops the candidate thinking, and the daughter’s urgency pushes towards a reflex prescription. The patterns below are the common failing routes, and each is fixable.

items.fail: Starting antibiotics because the dipstick was positive.
items.why: UKHSA advises against dipsticks over 65; up to half of older adults have asymptomatic bacteriuria. The prescription buries the real cause.
items.fix: Explain the dipstick’s limits, send urine for culture, and go on the history and examination.

items.fail: Never asking about bowels or the new painkiller.
items.why: Opioid-induced constipation with retention and overflow is the mechanism; missing it leaves the confusion and dribbling untreated.
items.fix: Ask every older person with new confusion about bowels, fluids and recent medication changes — and listen for “since those new painkillers”.

items.fail: Managing new confusion entirely by video.
items.why: Retention, faecal impaction and sepsis need hands-on assessment; remote-only care is unsafe here.
items.fix: Name the limits of video and arrange a same-day examination and bladder scan — framed as completing the job at home.

items.fail: Talking to Carol about Harold while he sits there.
items.why: It fails Relating to Others and misses his description (“it won’t come proper”) that unlocks the diagnosis.
items.fix: Greet him by name, ask his consent, and take his history in his own words first.

items.why: Derek’s death in hospital drives the antibiotic demand; unaddressed, she will resist any plan that sounds like admission.
items.fix: “That sounded personal — has something happened?” Then say plainly: “Everything we’re doing is designed to treat him at home.”

items.fail: A vague close — “call if he gets worse”.
items.why: Carol needs specific triggers she can act on tonight, and a frail man with delirium needs a named follow-up.
items.fix: Three named triggers (can’t pass urine, hard swollen belly, drowsy or feverish) and a call from you tomorrow afternoon.

timeMap.d: Greet Harold by name and get his consent. Carol pushes for antibiotics — acknowledge her worry and set an agenda: Harold first, then Carol.
Harold’s own words (“won’t come proper”), bowels (five days), abdominal discomfort, baseline, fever and drowsiness, fluid intake. Catch “since those new painkillers”.
Harold’s fear of not coping alone. Carol’s cracked voice leads to Derek — say out loud that the plan is to treat him at home.
Dipsticks are unreliable over 65; the constipation–retention mechanism; same-day exam and bladder scan with urine culture; stop co-codamol, laxative, fluid plan.
Can’t pass urine, hard swollen belly, drowsy or feverish — urgent call or 999. Named call tomorrow. Teach-back with Harold.

wordPics.pass: Explains that dipsticks are unreliable over 65, identifies constipation from co-codamol, arranges same-day examination and bladder scan, stops or reduces the opioid, and safety-nets.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: talks to Harold directly and gets the “won’t come proper” history; notices Carol’s cracked voice, finds Derek and says “we are treating him at home”; answers Harold’s leak fear with a fluid plan; closes with teach-back from Harold himself.

avoid.dont: “The dipstick is positive, so I’ll start some trimethoprim to be safe.”
avoid.instead: “Over 65, those sticks turn positive in lots of people with nothing wrong — his story tells us more.”
avoid.why: Treating a dipstick misses the real cause and exposes him to antibiotic harms.

avoid.dont: “Carol, how has your dad been sleeping?” (with Harold sitting there)
avoid.instead: “Harold, tell me in your own words what’s happening with the waterworks.”
avoid.why: Talking over him fails Relating to Others and misses the key history.

avoid.dont: “If he’s confused, he really needs to go into hospital.”
avoid.instead: “Everything we’re doing today — the examination, the scan, the laxatives — is how we treat this at home.”
avoid.why: It triggers Carol’s deepest fear and is not what the clinical picture requires.

I’m so sorry, Carol. That explains exactly why you want this sorted at home — and I want to be clear: everything I’m about to suggest is designed to treat Harold here, at home.
SCA_MODELS.why: Validates the loss and gives the reassurance she needs

SCA_MODELS.text: About the dipstick: over 65, those sticks are unreliable — up to half of older people have some bacteria in their urine without any infection. So I’d rather go on Harold’s story. And it points somewhere else. The new painkillers contain codeine, which bungs the bowels up. Five days of a full bowel can press on the bladder so it can’t empty; it overflows in little dribbles — the damp patches — and that backed-up system, plus not drinking, can fog his evenings.
SCA_MODELS.why: Defuses the dipstick and names the likely mechanism

SCA_MODELS.text: Carol: So it isn’t an infection?

It might not be, and antibiotics wouldn’t fix a blocked bowel or a full bladder. I can’t be sure over video, so I don’t want to guess. I’d like a doctor or nurse to see him in person this afternoon: feel his tummy, check the back passage, and scan his bladder. We’ll send a urine sample to the lab rather than rely on the stick, and do some bloods. That completes the job — it’s not sending him in.
SCA_MODELS.why: Names video limits; same-day exam, bladder scan, culture

SCA_MODELS.text: Carol: And if his bladder is full?

Then usually a nurse can pass a small tube to drain it, often at home or in the surgery, and the relief is quick. The wrong treatment is what would make hospital more likely — the right one keeps him here.
SCA_MODELS.why: Reframes antibiotics honestly against her fear

SCA_MODELS.text: Harold, the painkillers helped your shoulder but they’re causing this. I’d like to stop the co-codamol and use regular paracetamol with a rub-on anti-inflammatory gel for the shoulder instead. Would you be willing to try that?
SCA_MODELS.why: Acts on the drug cause with Harold’s agreement

SCA_MODELS.text: Harold: If it stops this, yes.

I’ll also start a laxative today to get the bowels moving. And the drinking — I know you’ve cut back to avoid leaking, but once the bladder can empty properly, drinking more should stop the dribbling, not cause it. Could we aim for a cup every couple of hours during the day, easing off in the evening?
SCA_MODELS.why: Fluid plan that answers his leak fear

SCA_MODELS.text: Harold: I can try.
Carol, could you or the carers keep a note of drinks and when his bowels open? And I’ll mark the co-codamol so it doesn’t get repeated automatically.
SCA_MODELS.why: Shares the plan and closes the prescribing loop

SCA_MODELS.text: Carol: Yes, I can do that.

Three things would change the plan tonight: if he can’t pass water at all, if his tummy becomes hard and swollen, or if he becomes drowsy, hot or shivery. Any of those — ring us straight away, or 111 or 999 out of hours. Otherwise I’ll ring you both tomorrow afternoon myself.
SCA_MODELS.why: Plain-language triggers and a named follow-up

SCA_MODELS.text: Carol: Thank you. I really thought you’d say hospital.
Harold, can you tell me in your own words what we’re going to do?
SCA_MODELS.why: Teach-back with the patient, not just the daughter

SCA_MODELS.text: Harold: Stop the new tablets, take the paracetamol, something for my bowels, drink more tea, and someone comes to feel my belly today.
Exactly that. Anything either of you wants to ask before we finish?
SCA_MODELS.why: Shares the floor with both

SCA_MODELS.text: Carol: No — thank you, doctor.

SCA_STEM.name: Harold Finch
meds: Co-codamol 30/500 four times daily (started 3 weeks ago by a locum for shoulder pain)
SCA_STEM.recent: Care agency dipsticked his urine yesterday — reported “positive”. Daughter Carol reports a week of strong-smelling urine, dribbling and increased confusion in the evenings. Two weeks ago independent: crossword, walking to the paper shop. Lives at home with a care agency; Carol visits daily.
SCA_STEM.reason: Urgent video consultation requested by his daughter, who wants antibiotics started today.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: UKHSA Diagnosis of urinary tract infections: quick reference tools for primary care (2025) · NICE CG103 — delirium · NICE NG109 — lower UTI prescribing · NICE NG253 — sepsis
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Over 65, a positive dipstick does not diagnose infection. New evening confusion, dribbling and five days’ constipation after starting co-codamol point to opioid-induced constipation with urinary retention and overflow, and early delirium. Hunt the cause, examine the same day, and send a urine culture rather than treating a dipstick.

points.t: UKHSA: urine dipsticks are not recommended in people aged 65 and over — up to half of older adults have bacteria in the urine without infection (asymptomatic bacteriuria), which does not need antibiotics. Smelly or dark urine alone is not a UTI and often reflects dehydration.

points.h: Use symptoms and signs — and look for other causes
points.t: UKHSA over-65 tool: consider UTI with new dysuria, or two or more of new frequency or urgency, new incontinence, new or worse delirium, suprapubic pain, visible haematuria, or fever. New dribbling and new confusion overlap with retention and constipation, so exclude other causes and send a urine sample for culture before any antibiotic.

NICE CG103: identify and manage the possible causes of delirium. Here: a new opioid, five days’ constipation, likely retention, poor fluid intake — plus infection to exclude. A structured tool such as the 4AT helps document it.

Codeine commonly causes constipation (BNF) and can contribute to urinary retention; faecal loading can also impair bladder emptying. Retention with overflow presents as frequent dribbling of small volumes. Same-day in-person assessment: abdomen, PR examination and a bladder scan.

Stop or step down the co-codamol — regular paracetamol (dose per BNF) with a topical NSAID for the shoulder; start a laxative such as macrogol (dose per BNF); a fluid plan that answers his fear of leaking; catheterise if there is a significant residual volume, with urology follow-up. Antibiotics per NICE NG109 only if culture and clinical picture support infection.
Inability to pass urine, a hard distended abdomen, or drowsiness, fever or rigors: same-day assessment, with sepsis risk judged per NICE NG253 — 999 if he appears seriously unwell.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Sought Harold’s consent and version first; acknowledged Carol’s request without acting on the dipstick.
Lives at home with carers and daily visits from Carol; previous independence; fear of losing it; Carol’s bereavement.
Picked up “not right since those new painkillers”, the rubbing of the lower abdomen, and Carol’s cracked voice.
Carol: dipstick means infection, fear of hospital after Derek, wants antibiotics. Harold: “my works are old”, fear of not coping alone, not to be talked over.
Same-day abdominal and PR examination, bladder scan; urine culture instead of dipstick; U&E, FBC, CRP, calcium, glucose.
Opioid-induced constipation with retention and overflow; dehydration; delirium; UTI or urosepsis; prostatic obstruction.
Asked about fever, rigors, drowsiness, falls and inability to pass urine; baseline cognition established.
Likely urinary retention with overflow due to opioid-induced constipation and poor fluid intake, with early delirium; infection not yet excluded.
No antibiotics on a dipstick; stop co-codamol, paracetamol and topical NSAID, laxative, fluid plan; catheter if retention confirmed.
Medication review so the opioid isn’t repeated; hydration and continence; support for Carol as carer.
Same-day review; named call tomorrow; clear triggers for urgent contact or 999.

social.t: Carol, 68, visits daily and is herself grieving a husband who died in hospital; her fear shapes every request. She is entitled to a carer’s assessment (Care Act 2014).
Until two weeks ago Harold managed with carers and walked to the shop; he fears incontinence means the end of living independently. Community continence services can help once the cause is fixed.

legal.t: Mental Capacity Act 2005: assume capacity; delirium can affect it, but capacity is decision-specific and fluctuates. Involve Harold in decisions and seek his consent to discuss his care with Carol.
Once he is well, a gentle conversation about lasting power of attorney and his wishes about hospital care may help both of them.

professional.t: GMC Good practice in prescribing and managing medicines and devices (2021): review new medicines for adverse effects. Record the reaction to co-codamol and stop it being repeated automatically; feed back to the locum without blame.
New confusion cannot be safely assessed by video alone — arranging a same-day face-to-face examination is part of good clinical care, not escalation.

community.t: Care agency (fluid and bowel chart), district or practice nurse for bladder scan and catheter care, community continence service, Carers UK and Age UK for support.

redFlags: Unable to pass urine, painful distended bladder or hard swollen abdomen — urgent same-day assessment
Fever, rigors, drowsiness or rapid decline — possible sepsis, assess per NICE NG253
New confusion — cause-hunt (drugs, constipation, retention, dehydration, infection) with a structured tool such as the 4AT

Harold restricts fluids to avoid leaking and fears losing independence

ice: Ideas: Carol — “positive dipstick means infection”; Harold — “my works are just old”
Concerns: Carol — hospital, after Derek; Harold — the end of managing alone
Expectations: Carol — antibiotics today, no hospital; Harold — not to be talked over

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Explain plainly: “The dipstick can’t tell us much at Harold’s age. His story points to the new painkillers — they’ve blocked his bowels, which can stop the bladder emptying so it dribbles, and that can make him muddled. We need to check that in person today.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Think of a blocked drain in the kitchen that makes the sink next to it back up and overflow. Unblock the drain — the bowels — and the sink — the bladder — can empty again.”

management.reflectIce: “Carol, after what happened to Derek, I understand why you want to avoid hospital. Everything we’re doing today is designed to treat your dad here, at home.”
management.psychosocial: Talk to Harold directly and answer his leak fear with a fluid plan; give Carol a practical role (fluid and bowel chart) and a named call tomorrow.
sharedPlan: Same-day in-person assessment: abdomen, PR, bladder scan; urine culture (not dipstick); U&E, FBC, CRP, calcium, glucose
Stop co-codamol; regular paracetamol and topical NSAID; laxative such as macrogol (dose per BNF); fluid plan
Catheter if significant retention, with follow-up; antibiotics per NICE NG109 only if culture and signs support infection
safetyNet: Can’t pass urine, hard swollen abdomen, drowsy, hot or shivery — ring urgently, 111 or 999 out of hours
Named GP call tomorrow afternoon; co-codamol removed from repeats

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is failed by the word “UTI”: it stops the candidate thinking, and the daughter’s urgency pushes towards a reflex prescription. The patterns below are the common failing routes, and each is fixable.

items.fail: Starting antibiotics because the dipstick was positive.
items.why: UKHSA advises against dipsticks over 65; up to half of older adults have asymptomatic bacteriuria. The prescription buries the real cause.
items.fix: Explain the dipstick’s limits, send urine for culture, and go on the history and examination.

items.fail: Never asking about bowels or the new painkiller.
items.why: Opioid-induced constipation with retention and overflow is the mechanism; missing it leaves the confusion and dribbling untreated.
items.fix: Ask every older person with new confusion about bowels, fluids and recent medication changes — and listen for “since those new painkillers”.

items.fail: Managing new confusion entirely by video.
items.why: Retention, faecal impaction and sepsis need hands-on assessment; remote-only care is unsafe here.
items.fix: Name the limits of video and arrange a same-day examination and bladder scan — framed as completing the job at home.

items.fail: Talking to Carol about Harold while he sits there.
items.why: It fails Relating to Others and misses his description (“it won’t come proper”) that unlocks the diagnosis.
items.fix: Greet him by name, ask his consent, and take his history in his own words first.

items.why: Derek’s death in hospital drives the antibiotic demand; unaddressed, she will resist any plan that sounds like admission.
items.fix: “That sounded personal — has something happened?” Then say plainly: “Everything we’re doing is designed to treat him at home.”

items.fail: A vague close — “call if he gets worse”.
items.why: Carol needs specific triggers she can act on tonight, and a frail man with delirium needs a named follow-up.
items.fix: Three named triggers (can’t pass urine, hard swollen belly, drowsy or feverish) and a call from you tomorrow afternoon.
